_method: Stratified sample: every 5th listing page, 20 records/page, pages 1-1405 (page 1405 = Aug 2023, the 3-year boundary). 300 pages fetched, 5620 unique records, 0 failures. Classification derived from the listing title, which encodes required privilege and weakness type.
_caveat: The 'unknown' auth bucket (2045) is not missing data so much as a titling convention: Wordfence omits a privilege prefix for classes where it is implied (CSRF is inherently a victim-privilege flaw; many Reflected XSS entries likewise). Treat per-class auth fractions as reliable only where the class commonly carries an explicit prefix.
_key_findings: Contributor+ Stored XSS (997 of 5620, ~18% of all records) is the single most common WordPress vulnerability pattern. Any audit tool that does not handle it well is missing the bulk of real findings.
Stored XSS overall (1786, 32%) plus Authorization Bypass (911, 16%) account for nearly half of everything disclosed.

Severity and frequency are inversely related. The highest average CVSS classes (Privilege Escalation 9.03, Auth Bypass 8.89, RCE 8.86) are comparatively rare, while the most frequent classes sit in the medium band. This is exactly why priority must be severity x exploitability x prevalence rather than any one axis.

Only 295 of 5620 records (5%) are CVSS-critical, but unauthenticated File Inclusion (200) and unauthenticated SQL Injection (119) are individually common enough to deserve high-confidence detection rules.

CSV Injection (1) and XXE (2) are rare in this listing, but NVD independently reports 25 CWE-1236 records over the same window; low counts here reflect classification convention more than true absence, so these classes are retained with lower priority rather than dropped.
